title: Inside the 280-line DGA classifier
author: olladns Security Team
excerpt: Why feature-based scoring still beats deep learning for resolver-side botnet detection — and how we keep it explainable.
content:
Most DNS security vendors either buy a black-box DGA feed or ship a multi-megabyte neural network. We chose a third path: a 280-line feature-based classifier that runs inline, explains every score, and costs essentially zero per query.

Why not a neural network?

Deep learning is seductive for DGA detection. LSTMs and Transformers can reach high accuracy on labeled corpora. But at resolver-side scale they bring three problems we couldn't accept:

  • Opacity: when a SOC analyst asks why a domain was blocked, "the model said so" is not an acceptable answer.
  • Cost: running inference per query adds latency and compute budget that grows with traffic.
  • Drift: DGAs evolve quickly; retraining and redeploying a model is slower than tuning a few thresholds.

The feature set

Our classifier extracts interpretable signals from the second-level domain string:

  • Shannon entropy: random-looking algorithmic domains score higher.
  • N-gram frequency: we compare character pairs against a corpus of legitimate domains.
  • Vowel ratio: human-readable names have more vowels than DGA output.
  • Length and digit count: most DGAs use fixed-length alphanumeric strings.
  • Consonant runs: long sequences of consonants are rare in real brand names.
// Simplified score combination
let score = entropy * 0.35
          + ngram_unlikelihood * 0.30
          + length_bias * 0.15
          + digit_ratio * 0.10
          + consonant_run * 0.10;

if (score > THRESHOLD) { flag_as_dga_suspect(); }

Making it tunable

Per-tenant thresholds let aggressive teams block at 0.75 while conservative teams wait for 0.95. Every flagged domain carries a JSON rationale so analysts can see the breakdown and tune accordingly.

Explainability is not a nice-to-have for DNS security. If you can't tell a customer why you blocked something, you shouldn't have blocked it.

Results so far

On our internal test set the classifier catches ~94% of known DGA families with a false-positive rate below 0.3% against top-1M benign domains. The model file is 12 KB. Inference time is sub-millisecond.

title: 54 MCP tools, generated from OpenAPI
author: olladns Product Team
excerpt: How we keep the MCP server in sync with every REST endpoint without writing wrappers by hand.
content:
Every REST endpoint we ship becomes an MCP tool automatically. Here is how we generate 54 tools from our OpenAPI spec and keep them in lockstep with the API.

The wrapper problem

Hand-writing MCP wrappers for every endpoint is a recipe for drift. Rename a field in the API and five editor integrations break. We wanted one source of truth: the OpenAPI spec served at /api/v1/openapi.json.

Generation pipeline

  • FastMCP reads the OpenAPI spec at build time.
  • Each operation becomes a tool with typed arguments from the spec's schemas.
  • We annotate scope requirements from the x-required-scopes extension.
  • Five hand-curated workflows combine multiple tools for common tasks.

Result

When we add a new REST endpoint, the MCP tool appears in the next deploy without anyone writing a wrapper. The same validation, the same auth, the same audit logging applies whether the caller is curl, a dashboard, or Claude.

title: Designing scoped API keys for agents
author: olladns Engineering
excerpt: Tokens for CI, SIEM, and AI editors share the same auth surface but carry different audit fingerprints.
content:
CI pipelines, SIEM connectors, and AI agents all need API access, but they should not share the same key. Here is how we built scoped tokens that keep each workload inside its lane.

One auth surface, many actors

We use the same auth middleware for humans and machines, but the token metadata differs. A CI key carries scopes like policies:write and devices:read. A SIEM key gets analytics:read and audit:read. An AI editor key might only get threats:read and policies:write.

Fingerprinting every call

Every audit log row records the api_key_id that made the call, not just the user who created it. That means when Claude blocks a domain through MCP, the log shows it was the agent key — traceable, revocable, and scoped.

Rotation and expiry

Scoped keys support expiry dates and last-used timestamps. We surface stale keys in the dashboard so security teams can revoke what they forgot.

title: Why DNS filtering is the cheapest zero-trust control
author: olladns Security Team
excerpt: Every device on your network asks DNS before it connects anywhere. That makes the resolver the most universal enforcement point you already own.
content:
Zero-trust architectures usually start with identity and endpoints. That's backwards. Every device on your network already reports every destination to DNS — making the resolver the cheapest, most universal enforcement point you own.

The resolver sees everything

Before a laptop, server, printer, or IoT sensor connects to anything, it resolves a name. Malware beacons, phishing pages, and command-and-control servers all appear first as DNS queries. Blocking at the resolver stops the connection before any TCP handshake happens.

Why it's cheaper than EDR or SWG

  • No agent: point the device at a DoH/DoT resolver and policy applies instantly.
  • No traffic steering: you don't need to proxy every byte through a cloud SWG.
  • Universal coverage: works for unmanaged devices, guest networks, and IoT that can't run endpoint software.

What good DNS filtering actually blocks

The best DNS security layers stop phishing infrastructure within minutes of registration, identify algorithmic domains before they're on any threat feed, and catch lookalike domains targeting your brand specifically. That's the layer we are building at olladns.

title: Catching Cyrillic homoglyphs in 230 lines
author: olladns Security Team
excerpt: A Damerau-Levenshtein approach to brand impersonation that runs inline at DNS query time.
content:
Typosquatting is not just about misspellings anymore. Attackers now use Cyrillic homoglyphs to make evil domains look identical to trusted brands. Our 230-line detector runs at query time.

From ASCII to confusables

A domain like paypa-l.com is easy to catch with edit distance. But раурӑl.com, where the Latin a is replaced by Cyrillic а, defeats naive string comparison while looking identical to most users.

Normalization first

We normalize Unicode confusables to a canonical ASCII form before scoring. Internationalized domain names are decoded from Punycode, then each character is mapped to its closest ASCII homoglyph if one exists.

Edit distance against the protect-list

After normalization, we compute Damerau-Levenshtein distance against the tenant's protect-list. Domains within a tunable threshold are flagged as typosquats. The whole operation runs inline at ingest time.
